slides.title: Can better handoffs make an RLM more reliable?
slides.notes:
SAY: A handoff means passing a smaller task to a helper model and getting its answer back. Last time, we taught a basic Python routine. Now we study a routine using helpers and a separate reading test.

FOCUS: Can changing the RLM program make complete solutions more reliable?

CAUTION: The training and matching results are separate studies, not one learning curve.

slides.title: An RLM divides a large task into smaller steps.
slides.notes:
SAY: We want each user's count of questions asking for a location. Oslo and Kyoto qualify; Hamlet asks for a person. Helpers identify question types; Python counts: Ada one, Ben one.

WHY: The main model can inspect a file without reading it all at once. Helpers can divide work again.

CAUTION: This invented example explains the workflow, not a demonstrated ability to plan any unfamiliar task.

slides.title: Training taught a more reliable routine for asking helpers and calculating answers.
slides.notes:
SAY: Two copies learned the ask-and-calculate routine from different example sets. Success needs the right final answer and the requested calculation from actual helper replies. On 72 test tasks, successes were 12 before, then 55 or 53.

IF ASKED: Missing outcomes allow 12–19, 55, and 53–55. This is not sequential training.

CAUTION: New records, familiar task types; the helper remained fixed.

slides.title: We changed how helper answers are linked to the text they describe.
slides.notes:
SAY: This is a separate reading test. Maya bought a red bike: a vehicle follows from the text; a blue bike contradicts it. A name links each statement to its answer.

IF ASKED: The real task also allows not enough information. Software supplies names and format, not correct answers. Without names, order supplies the link.

TRANSITION: Does this help when one request contains many statements?

slides.title: Matching names helped helpers judge many statements in one request.
slides.notes:
SAY: Qwen and Mistral are two language models. Read left to right as each request contains more statements to judge. At 64, matching names raised Qwen from 44% to 83%, and Mistral from 35% to 52%.

IF ASKED: Same 16 input sets; 160 requests per model shown. Three invalid Mistral responses count wrong.

CAUTION: These are helper judgments, not complete RLM solutions. Backup 6 adds row numbers.

slides.title: Smaller requests were faster than large requests with matching names in this local test.
slides.notes:
SAY: All methods judged the same 768 statements. Each time covers that whole workload, not one request. Large named requests scored 85% in 91 seconds; one statement at a time scored 87% in 31 seconds.

IF ASKED: Up to four requests ran at once. Sixteen per request was faster but less accurate.

CAUTION: One-at-a-time sent about 2.5 times as much input as large named requests. This is a local tradeoff.

slides.title: Next test: let the RLM program organize helper requests and match their answers.
slides.notes:
SAY: Add a program component to group input items, preserve their names, and match replies. Compare fixed group sizes against the current RLM and one item per request.

IF ASKED: Current ask_batch matches whole requests. This would track individual items inside each request. Learning when to resize groups comes later.

CAUTION: No complete-RLM benefit is established. Matching names is standard and cannot ensure correct reading.

slides.title: We have a promising handoff result and a focused next research question.
slides.notes:
SAY: Training improved a routine; matching names improved helper reading. I recommend a focused whole-task study of the handoff procedure.

DISCUSS: Is this a worthwhile contribution? Which realistic task would make a convincing test?

STOP: This ends the ten-minute main talk. Remaining slides are optional answers to questions, not more required presentation.

slides.title: Example: the helper identifies question types, and Python adds the relevant points.
slides.notes:
SAY: Count only points attached to questions asking for a location. Ada gets four plus three, or seven. Ben gets two, not the six attached to his person question. Only Ada exceeds five: one user.

IF ASKED: The helper classifies; Python adds and compares. Wrong classifications can spoil correct arithmetic.

CAUTION: This is invented, not a copied training example. Assigned points are called weights in the experiment.

slides.title: Using the same name on a statement and its answer helped more than using different names.
slides.notes:
SAY: This tests whether any extra names help, or whether matching matters. Both versions had names and valid formatting. On later judgments, matching raised accuracy from 32.6% to 78.8%.

IF ASKED: Answer order still specified the intended statement, even with different names.

CAUTION: Last 32 judgments per 48-statement request; different input sets from slide 5. This does not explain the model's internal mechanism.

slides.title: Reward training did not improve the final-answer count in this trial.
slides.notes:
SAY: Reward training scores the model's attempts and adjusts its learned behavior. We tried correct-answer reward alone, then a separate run adding agreement with Python's calculation from helper replies. Neither improved the test count.

IF ASKED: Each attempted 576 practice solutions. Together they took about four hours and 39 minutes. Two missing tests explain 55–57.

CAUTION: Final numbers only; calculation review is unfinished.

slides.title: Training also helped with new combinations of familiar steps.
slides.notes:
SAY: First select users using their location questions. Then count their number questions, which are different records. The prompt gave both steps. Training raised verified successes from two to 29 out of 72.

IF ASKED: The combination was absent from our examples; the input sets were reused.

CAUTION: Missing results allow 2–13 versus 29–30. We checked calculations, not just easy-to-guess zeros. This is not inventing a plan.

slides.title: Misleading names can draw an answer toward the wrong input.
slides.notes:
SAY: Imagine being told to answer row seven but label it row eight. That name points to another text in the request. Accuracy was 39% with such misleading names, versus 80% with unrelated names.

IF ASKED: Order still told the model which statement to judge. Software forced the answer names.

CAUTION: Deliberate stress test, not normal use. We observed output behavior, not the model's attention.

slides.title: Both row numbers and arbitrary names helped when helpers judged many statements together.
slides.notes:
SAY: This adds the third comparison omitted from slide five: use matching row numbers rather than arbitrary names. Both helped the two language models judge statements.

IF ASKED: At 64 statements, Qwen scored 44%, 85%, 83%; Mistral 35%, 58%, 52%. Order: no names, row numbers, arbitrary names.

CAUTION: Three Mistral arbitrary-name responses had invalid formatting. Do not conclude row numbers are inherently better.
